title: One tree, one week
hook: visit the same tree daily, and let one tree teach you how much changes in a week
carry: something ordinary becomes someone you visit

segments.voice: Yesterday, panta rhei, as we watched the clouds, and your line was never the same. Did a cloud change shape while you were looking at it? Today we trade the moving sky for something that stays put. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

There's probably a tree you pass without seeing it. On the way to the bus, outside the office window, at the corner where the dog always stops. It's easy to know a phone's lock screen better than that tree. That's not a flaw. It's just how attention works: what stays still, we stop looking at. Clouds get our eyes because they move. A tree seems to do nothing at all. Today's practice turns that around. Not a new tree. Not a famous one. The same one, every day, for a week.
screen: `THE TREE YOU PASS.` → `WHAT STAYS STILL, WE STOP SEEING.` → `THE SAME ONE, EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the tree that seems to stand still. It only seems that way. Over a week a tree is busy: a bud swells, a leaf turns, a branch holds a bird on Monday and is empty on Tuesday, the light hits it from a new angle as the season tips. You won't see any of it in a single glance. You'll see it by coming back. Second, trees in the old texts. The very first psalm has a tree in it. The person who delights in the law, the psalm says, "shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season." Notice the words in his season. The psalm doesn't picture a tree that fruits all year. It pictures one that keeps its own time, and stays rooted while it waits. Third, the tree as a place to sit. Buddhist tradition tells of Siddhartha sitting beneath a tree, resolved not to get up until he understood, and awakening there. That tree became known as the bodhi tree, the tree of awakening. In the story, the tree doesn't teach him anything. It simply holds still while he does. Fourth, why one tree and not many. A walk in the woods is wonderful, but it's a sampler. One tree is a relationship. By day three you know where the bark is torn. By day five you notice that the same branch catches the evening light. Something ordinary becomes someone you visit. That shift, from scenery to a companion, is a small doorway into awe.
screen: `A TREE ONLY SEEMS TO STAND STILL.` · `PSALM 1: A TREE BY THE WATER.` · `THE TREE OF AWAKENING.` · `ONE TREE IS A RELATIONSHIP.` · then, large: `IN HIS SEASON.`

segments.voice: Today is the first visit. If you can, go to a window or a doorway where a tree is in sight, or step outside to one. If no tree is near, choose one in your memory, a tree you know well. Look at it as if you'll be asked to draw it tomorrow. The shape of the trunk. Where the biggest branch leaves it. The color of the light on the leaves, or on the bare twigs. Let your breathing slow while you look. You don't need to think anything about it. Just meet it. The bell holds the time.
One tree. The same tree, visited day after day, until something you walked past becomes something you know. Today's word.
Your line: something ordinary becomes someone you visit. Pick your tree today and visit it again tomorrow, at about the same hour. Notice one thing that's different. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Some people keep a practice of returning to the same tree or spot outdoors over days or seasons, noticing how it changes; trees also appear as images of rootedness in the Psalms and as the place of awakening in Buddhist tradition.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakening. Buddhist tradition calls the tree Siddhartha sat beneath the bodhi tree.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tree is scenery: it stands there and does nothing.
what it means: one tree, visited daily, turns out to be busy: buds, birds, light, season.
what a scholar hears: the first psalm's tree bears fruit "in his season", rooted while it waits, and the Buddhist story sets awakening beneath a tree.
